deep.reconstruction:
This page is a draft of the opening, preliminary section of Riemann's paper on linear differential equations with algebraic coefficients. The headings read 'Zwei allgemeine Lehrsätze über lineare Differentialgleichungen' and 'Allgemeine Voraussetzungen und Hülfsmittel für die Untersuchung von Functionen vielfach veränderlicher Größen'. It is the posthumously published fragment of 1857, Werke XXI. The previous page discusses monodromy systems, how they depend on the branch points, and counts of arbitrary constants; this page lays down the function-theoretic foundations for that. There are no computations, only definitions and quoted theorems.

(1) Single-valued branch. A branch of a function of x is called 'einwerthig' (single-valued) in a neighbourhood of a value a if, for all x with |x-a|<r (some finite r>0), there corresponds a determinate value of that same branch that varies continuously with x.

The same definition is given for several variables: single-valued near a point (a_1,...,a_m) means a determinate, continuously varying value of the branch on a polydisc-like neighbourhood of finite size.

(2) Branches. If y takes several values y', y'', y''' for one x, then each value, continued with x varying continuously, forms a branch of y.

(3) Branch value. A value (point) at which one branch connects to another is called a Verzweigungswerth (branch point). A small sketch of a branching path is drawn beside this.

(4) The complex plane. The now 'generally known' geometric representation is assumed: z = x+iy is identified with the point with rectangular coordinates (x,y) in an infinite plane, and the quantity and its point are denoted by the same letter.

(5) Definition of a function of x+iy. A function of x+iy is any quantity w that varies with z according to i dw/dx = dw/dy. The first, crossed-out draft has dw/dx = dw/(i dy), which is equivalent. Riemann explicitly does not presuppose any analytic expression of w in x and y; this is his 1851 dissertation definition (Cauchy-Riemann equations as the definition of analyticity).

(6) Taylor expansion (quoted as 'a known theorem'). If w has a determinate, continuously varying value everywhere in a neighbourhood of a, then w = sum_{n>=0} a_n (z-a)^n there. This representability holds up to the distance from a at which a discontinuity occurs, i.e. the radius of convergence is at least the distance to the nearest singularity.

(7) Uniqueness. By the reasoning behind the method of undetermined coefficients, w is completely determined once it is given on an arbitrarily small piece around a. Combining this with (6) (implicitly by analytic continuation along chains of discs, my filling), a function of x+iy in a region of the plane is completely determined once it is given along a finite line (arc) in the interior of that region. This is the identity theorem.

Purpose: these are the 'general assumptions and tools' needed to define the branches y_1,...,y_n, their branch points and their linear substitutions in the main theorems about linear ODEs.
errors: No mathematical errors. The equation i*dw/dx = dw/dy is correct for w holomorphic in z = x+iy, and so is the cancelled variant dw/dx = dw/(i dy).

Step (7), from 'determined in a small piece around a' to 'determined by values on a finite arc in a region', silently uses connectedness of the region and analytic continuation. It also uses the fact that values on an arc determine all derivatives at a point (or that zeros of a nonzero power series are isolated). This is standard but not argued.

The single-valuedness definition requires only continuity of the branch; differentiability (the Cauchy-Riemann condition) is assumed separately. As stated, the Taylor theorem in (6) needs w to be a 'function of x+iy' in the sense of (5), not merely continuous. This is implicit in context.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the known preliminary section of Riemann's 1857 fragment 'Zwei allgemeine Lehrsätze über lineare Differentialgleichungen mit algebraischen Coefficienten' (Werke). It restates standard foundations he had already given in his 1851 dissertation: the Cauchy-Riemann definition, Taylor expansion and the identity theorem. Only the drafting variants (e.g. the explicit several-variable definition of single-valuedness) are of minor philological interest.

checkable.asserts: A polynomial in z = x+iy satisfies Riemann's defining equation i dw/dx = dw/dy
conj(z) does not satisfy the equation, so it is not a 'function of x+iy' in Riemann's sense
The cancelled variant dw/dx = dw/(i dy) is equivalent to the final form
The Taylor coefficients of 1/(1-z) about a give convergence radius |1-a|, the distance from a to the singularity z=1 (check at a numeric value of a)

transcription_corrections: The final definition reads 'i dw/dx = dw/dy' as transcribed. The earlier cancelled attempt appears to read 'dw/dx = dw/(i dy)' (the transcription gives it this way); the i in the denominator is faint in the image.

The phrase 'bei [-Punkt-]' before 'an welchem Zweige sich ein Zweig...' should read 'Der Werth, bei welchem sich ein Zweig einer Function an einen anderen Zweig anschließt'. 'Werth' is the inserted replacement for cancelled 'Punkt'.
'von denen ich bei ihrer Behandlung ausgegangen werde' is probably 'ausgegangen bin' or 'ausgehen werde'; the reading is uncertain.
The series is written as Σ_{n=0}^{n=∞} a_n (z-a)^n, with summation limits written as n=0 and n=∞; this matches the image.
The '[Figur]' is a small sketch of a curve branching, drawn next to the branch-point definition.
The heading 'Zwei allgemeine Lehrsätze über' appears twice: a first incomplete version followed by the full title 'Zwei allgemeine Lehrsätze über lineare Differentialgleichungen'.
